#4528. Are Ultra-Processed Foods Raising Your Risk of Stroke and Obesity?

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

High intakes of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) have been linked to multiple adverse health outcomes, including an increased risk of stroke, heart disease, cancer, and obesity.

A recent study published in JAMA Open Network showed that a higher intake of UPFs may be linked to brain damage and could lead to an increased risk of stroke and cognitive decline later in life.

Another large study in Family Medicine and Community Health found that people who consumed the most UPFs were at a higher risk of developing chronic diseases, such as diabetes, obesity, heart disease, and cancer.

An earlier review in Nature Metabolism also showed that fructose in UPFs may contribute to obesity and metabolic diseases.

Together, these studies add to research on the effects of eating high levels of UPFs on your health.

A recent study published in JAMA Network Open found that healthy adults who eat higher levels of UPFs may be more likely to experience damage to their brain that could increase the risk of stroke and future memory problems.

The cross-sectional study analyzed 8,783 adults between the ages of 35 and 69 without cardiovascular disease. The researchers used MRI scans to evaluate participants’ brains and measured UPF intake using a food frequency questionnaire.

UPFs accounted for an average of 25% of participants’ diet. However, among those with the highest intake, these foods accounted for 45% of their daily intake, compared with 16% among those with the lowest intake.

When comparing the highest intake to the lowest, the researchers found that those in the higher group had 1.7% more body fat and had a higher risk of vascular brain injury (VBI).

The findings suggest that there may be a link between high UPF intake and brain changes that could increase the risk of stroke and cognitive decline.

“These findings are concerning, but it is important to remember that an association does not prove cause and effect,” Michelle Routhenstein, a preventive cardiology dietitian at Entirely Nourished, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline in a previous interview.

“While we can’t conclude from this study that limiting UPFs would improve brain health, we have decades of literature demonstrating that higher intakes of green leafy vegetables, brightly colored fruits, whole grains, and lean protein sources are good for brain health,” Suzanne Judd, PhD, director of the UC College of Medicine’s Center for Public Health, who wasn’t involved in the study, previously told Healthline.

Routhenstein advised starting simply with one manageable swap to help lower your UPF intake.

“I want people to feel empowered, not fearful, when making food choices,” she said. “Healthy eating does not mean having to cook everything from scratch. What matters most is building consistent, nourishing habits that support both heart and brain health.”

A large recent study published in Family Medicine and Community Health found that people who ate the most UPFs were more likely to develop chronic diseases, such as:

It also found that these individuals may have a higher overall risk of death.

The research team analyzed 51 studies involving nearly 9 million participants from around the world, with follow-up periods ranging from 2 to 32 years.

They found that consuming high levels of UPFs was associated with an increased risk of many chronic health issues.

Those with the highest levels of UPF consumption showed a:

These numbers were derived by comparing people who ate the most UPFs with those who ate the least.

Johannah Katz, MA, a registered dietitian at Nourish, who was not involved in the study, told Healthline in a previous interview that there isn’t currently a cutoff point at which ultra-processed foods become harmful.

“What this new research suggests is more of a dose-response relationship; the more ultra-processed food in the diet, the higher the observed risk for several chronic diseases,” she said.

Reducing UPF intake may help decrease these risks.

A recent review published in Nature Metabolism highlighted the role fructose can play in driving disease, distinct from its role as a source of calories.

Fructose is a simple sugar that is found both naturally, in fruits and honey, and in sweeteners like high fructose corn syrup and sucrose (table sugar).

One reason that fructose can be problematic is that it has twice the sweetness of glucose, which can lead to increased cravings for more fructose-containing foods and drinks.

“Fructose found in these processed forms is not handled the same way as regular blood sugar,” Routhestein, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline in a previous interview. “When it is consumed, it goes to the liver, where it easily turns into fat, which can build up in the liver and around the organs and contribute to conditions like fatty liver and metabolic syndrome.”

This recent review highlights how fructose metabolism bypasses key steps in energy-processing pathways. This can lead to various effects, such as:

“The emerging body of research suggests that fructose is not metabolically identical to all other carbohydrates, especially when it is consumed in excess through sugar-sweetened beverages and ultra-processed foods,” Serena Poon, certified nutritionist & longevity wellness advisor, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline in a previous interview.

“Excess calories still matter, but fructose may affect metabolism differently than other sugars, particularly in the liver … In my view, this supports a more nuanced conversation because it is not just about sugar in the abstract, but also about the form, dose, and dietary context in which fructose is consumed,” she said.

#4527. Tesla launches FSD v15, targets its biggest weaknesses, from signs to potholes

Tesla has started rolling out “Full Self-Driving” v15, and its list of improvements reads like a list of FSD’s biggest current weaknesses: sign detection, potholes, and speed handling in school zones.

Tesla also claims “25x better handling of safety critical cases” and is adding a new live visualization that looks seriously impressive. If the driving improvements are as real as the visuals, this is a big update.

Tesla announced the rollout on X this afternoon, and its Tesla Super Intelligence account followed up with the full release notes. The company didn’t say which vehicles get it first, but it has previously told investors that its AI4 (HW4) computer is enough to run v15.

Here are Tesla’s release notes for FSD v15:

v15 upgrades every part of the end-to-end driving network. Includes:

Tesla’s main announcement also says FSD can now slow down for speed cameras, and it adds Bike Rack Mode, which allows FSD with a bike rack or a similar hitch accessory. Navigation learning only covers the start and end of trips for now; Tesla says later v15 releases will expand it to the entire route.

The new visualization is the flashiest part, and based on the video Tesla shared, it’s super impressive. The center screen shows a detailed, rendered version of the street around the car, far beyond the current FSD visualization.

FSD v15 now starting to roll out – upgrading every part of the end-to-end driving network Safety25x better handling of safety critical casesTesla Reality View Adds a live visualization of the drive that lets you see & control what FSD is planning to doNavigation for start… pic.twitter.com/Sfjk4wZecW

Tesla calls it “Reality View” in its announcement and “Tesla Augmented Reality” in the release notes. The notes say it replaces all the separate model signals with a single end-to-end visualization that uses less compute, and Tesla says it lets the driver “see & control what FSD is planning to do.” If that works as advertised, it could make supervising the system a lot easier.

What stands out more is where Tesla is focusing. Almost every driving improvement in the release notes targets an area where FSD struggles today.

Signs are a big one. In a test published in September, Brussels nonprofit Johanna.be found that FSD exceeded the limit in 55% of the 30 km/h zones it drove through, averaging 44 km/h. In most of those zones, the car’s screen showed a 50 km/h limit. It didn’t read the sign.

Potholes are another. In August, Musk said pothole avoidance was “coming soon”, something he had already promised back in 2019. Today, FSD still drives straight through them.

School zones are on the list too. NHTSA is reviewing a petition claiming Tesla’s Robotaxis speed through active school zones, on top of an investigation it opened in October 2025 into FSD traffic-law violations like running red lights. Slowing for speed cameras fits the same theme, though it also suggests Tesla is fine with FSD going over the limit when there’s no camera around.

So if v15 really fixes these, it’s a very good update. The question is by how much.

One change goes the other way. Tesla says it is “decreasing strictness” of driver monitoring in higher-speed driver profiles, at a time when sleeping drivers on FSD keep making headlines and Tesla is tightening monitoring in Europe at regulators’ request.

The release notes clear up what the “25x” refers to: Tesla says the new vision encoder improves the critical intervention rate by 25x. That’s the right metric to measure progress toward unsupervised driving. But Tesla still doesn’t share the actual number, only the multiplier.

The math gets interesting fast. Our data from earlier this year suggested FSD v14 could go a couple thousand miles between critical interventions. A 25x improvement on that would put v15 around 50,000 miles between critical interventions, well beyond the roughly 10,000 miles we’ve said Tesla needs for a limited unsupervised service. If that were true across the fleet, we could see Tesla having its most meaningful push toward autonomy in a long time.

And v15 already carries plenty of hype. In April, Elon Musk wrote that v15 “will far exceed human levels of safety, even in completely unsupervised and complex situations.” We pointed out at the time that he had said similar things about v12 and v14. In August, Tesla told JPMorgan that v15 is a “step-change” built on seven “core technologies,” with about 40% of them already running in its Robotaxi fleet in Austin.

FSD has never improved in a straight line. Every major version has brought real gains along with new problems, and point releases regularly go backward.

When v14 arrived in October 2025, it came with hallucinations, brake stabbing, and excessive speeding, and early crowdsourced data showed about 732 miles between critical disengagements, below what we expected. It then improved a lot. Then the v14.2 updates went backward before Musk sold v14.3 as the version where “the last big piece of the puzzle finally lands.”

Seven months and a long string of point releases later, owners are still supervising, and Tesla now needs v15 to deliver what v14.3 was supposed to.

I remain skeptic of Tesla's autonomous driving until they apply for the California DMV permit to begin testing autonomous driving without a driver. California is a big enough of a potential market for robotaxi that Tesla is operating a human driver taxi service. The common presumption is that Tesla is avoiding California autonomous testing because it requires disclosing critical interventions and other data which wouldn't be favorable to Tesla's claims.

The visuals are super impressive. That much we can already judge from the video, and Reality View could make FSD easier to understand and supervise.

The driving side is harder to judge. Tesla is going straight at the weaknesses that owners and regulators complain about most: misread speed limits, potholes, school zones, debris. If v15 delivers real progress on all of those, it’s a really good update.

But “improved detection” doesn’t tell us how much better, and a 25x multiplier without the underlying number is hard to check. FSD has gone two steps forward, one step back throughout its history, with point releases regularly breaking things the previous version handled fine. And Tesla still won’t publish the disengagement data that would settle it.

#4525. Ancient Egyptian curse found in 3,400-year-old trash heap

🛍️ Live: The best Black Friday deals on stuff you actually want 🛍️

Published Nov 24, 2026 12:24 PM EST

A well-known ancient Egyptian curse is not only older than historians thought—the curse that called upon the sun god’s wrath upon one’s enemies was much more commonly employed than experts assumed. However, the new evidence concerning the “Apophis ritual” wasn’t recently discovered in an excavated spellbook. According to a study published in the Journal of the Egyptian Language and Antiquities, archaeologists learned the latest details from postage stamp-sized papyrus fragments left in 3,400-year-old trash piles.

Prior to finding the 40 charred remnants, the only documentation of the Apophis ritual was a ritual manual dating back to the late fourth century BCE. Egyptian priests originally designed the spell to aid the sun god Ra against Apophis, his eternal foe and the snake god of chaos, fire, and darkness. Others later adapted the ritual to curse enemies of the pharaoh and counter problems associated with the serpent like inclement weather and poisons. But although researchers initially assumed the Apophis ritual was reserved for religious leaders, the papyrus fragments retrieved from temple ruins at Thebes have dramatically expanded its audience.

“They show that the ritual was much older than the one surviving copy from the fourth century [BCE] might suggest,” Fredrik Hagen, an Egyptologist at the University of Copenhagen and study co-author, said in a statement. “Already 1,000 years earlier, during what we call the New Kingdom, it was an integrated part of Egyptian culture.”

While additional analysis of the fragments revealed that such rituals were widespread in ancient Egypt, Hagen explained that additional contextual references to the Apophis incantation indicate it was a “common feature” in daily life.

“We know that literate people, including those who were not priests, had access to magical rituals and functioned as magicians and healers,” he said. “It is clear that people approached scribes for help in performing magic, both for protection and for attacking others.”

The existence of the remnants are surprising in their own right, given what the ritual required. Their charring is only part of the necessary curse protocols—prior to burning the written spells, practitioners stepped on the papyrus, stabbed it with a knife, and even spit on it.

“For the ritual to be successful, the materials had to be destroyed by fire, so we are extremely fortunate to have found any of them in a condition that still allows them to be recognized and studied,” said Hagen.

#4524. Here are 7 great reasons rural drivers SHOULD embrace EVs in 2027

America’s heartland is full of rural communities that are miles away from its major cities, both geographically and culturally – but that doesn’t mean these more sparsely populated regions can’t reap the benefits of electrification. In fact, EVs offer rural drivers even more benefits than they do to city-dwellers!

UPDATE 21NOV2026: this is an annual (ish) post I have been updating since 2024.

“An electric lifestyle would be a boon to our rural heartland,” wrote the Union of Concerned Scientists’ Maria Cecilia Pinto de Moura. “Rural communities across the country have their own distinguishing characteristics, but certain shared characteristics such as driving distances, the type of vehicles driven, and socio-economics are factors which contribute to this larger potential to benefit from vehicle electrification.”

Pinto de Moura went on to outline five ways rural and country drivers could benefit from going electric – but that was in 2021, and a whole lot has changed in the nearly six years since. As such, I thought it was high time we revisit some of the reasons EVs are a great fit for rural lifestyles, see if we could uncover any new ones, and outline the reasons we think rural drivers should rush to embrace electric vehicles in the coming calendar year.

When you hear that line about, “the average American drives 30 to 40 miles a day,” remember that in towns like Wellington, Ohio, or Colfax, Washington, 30 miles is a grocery run. Each way. So when people trot out that old line about range anxiety, what rural drivers actually hear isn’t reassurance. It’s dismissal — a suggestion that they drive too far for an EV to work, when nothing could be further from the truth.

A recent study by Rural Climate Partnership found that rural drivers spend an average of 44% more on fuel than city dwellers, and that the top 3.6% of rural drivers — the “supermilers” who rack up the most miles — could save over $4,000 each year by switching to electric fuel.

Country guys and gals love their pickups, and arguably the biggest difference between the EV market of 2021 and 2027 is that electric trucks and SUVs are no longer a novelty. There are now battery-powered options ready to haul, handle chores, head out camping, and tow a trailer.

What’s more, a new wave of more affordable electric trucks from Ford, Slate, and others is challenging the idea that you need a $50,000 half-ton pickup to get real work done. Early interest suggests there’s plenty of pent-up demand for capable, accessible electric work trucks that don’t need to be twenty feet long or cost more than what your parent’s paid for their house.

With only about 45% of rural counties having access to DC fast charging, public charging still isn’t as visible as many first-time EV buyers might like, but it’s far better than it used to be — and improving fast. Still, that’s not the real EV advantage. Home charging is.

Unlike many apartment-dwelling urban drivers, most rural owners can charge right at home. More than 80% of rural households have a driveway or garage that are ideal for overnight Level 2 charging, and many already have a 240V outlet, keeping setup costs (if there even are any) to a minimum.

Plug in before bed, wake up to a full battery every morning, and do it for pennies on the dollar, especially with off-peak rates.

If disaster strikes and you lose power, your EV could be more than just a way to get around. Many electric cars and trucks have the ability to power refrigerators, freezers, well pumps, lights, and other household essentials for days, either through onboard outlets or a dedicated vehicle-to-home (V2H) system that feeds electricity directly into your home’s electrical panel. Ford’s from-the-ashes F-150 Lightning and Tesla’s Cybertruck are already among the EVs making that capability a reality, and newer, more affordable electric trucks promise to bring V2H tech to even more households.

If you live in an area prone to extreme weather, where severe storms, hurricanes, or wildfires can leave homes without electricity for days, that’s a pretty compelling benefit. Keeping food cold, medical equipment running or essential medication refrigerated can be a literal lifesaver – and your EV’s battery might be the biggest backup power source you own.

It’s been a few years since a working class guy could reasonably expect to get a new pickup for less than $50,000. And, while much has been made of the “high cost of electric vehicles,” the truth is that thanks to killer lease deals, new tax incentives, and companies like Ford Pro and TRC that are willing to help you find even more funding to help pay for them, EVs can often be had for less than a comparable gas model.

As such, getting behind the wheel of an ultra-powerful, ultra smooth-running electric pickup truck from your favorite brand is easier than ever.

At the risk of sounding like a paranoid red hat, rural Americans are proud Americans – just like rural Canadians are proud Canadians. Unfortunately, every gallon of gas burned in their pickups and SUVs came from oil drilled, refined, and traded on global markets — and that means supporting the oil business and economies of nations whose values don’t always align with, or maybe are even outright hostile to theirs.

Switching to an EV can help more of that money right here at home, especially as more and better battery recycling efforts come online and newer battery and anode/cathode chemistries are developed, reducing dependence on rare Earth metals, cobalt, and even lithium.

Even better, thanks to the rapid expansion and dramatically reduced costs of wind and solar power, you can power your EV with energy that is 100% Made in the USA, that doesn’t support foreign oil interests or involve you in a bunch of dumb oil wars (except indirectly), and which creates good-paying construction and maintenance jobs for local workers.

In my experience, rural buyers appreciate things that last, and are moved more by lasting quality than fleeting fashions – and that’s exactly why they should be looking at EVs.

We recently covered a 2019 Chevy Bolt that had put more than 470,000 miles on its odometer, along with data from Ford showing its battery packs maintain more than 90% of their battery health after 100,000 miles.

And while we’re talking about data, it should be noted that EVs aren’t some new, unknown technology. The first modern high-voltage car battery hit the road more than 30 years ago (the Prius was released in 1996, as a 1997 model). Some of those cars are still on the road – and there are literally tens of thousands of EVs out there still performing their daily driver duties every day.

There are obviously more reasons to go electric than these, from lower cost of ownership to saving the planet to absolutely killer burnouts that would make the one-tire-fire era IROC Camaros hang their 305s in shame – but I think those kind of fade into the background as being appealing to just about everyone, instead of being especially appealing to rural drivers.

I live in rural Australia in a village that doesn't even have a fuel bowser. My shopping trip is usually around 164km (100miles). I have solar on my roof. I now have an EV (one of the Chinese brands that aren't available in the USA) and am delighted with it. I'm saving a lot of money on fuel and because the solar feed-in tariff goes negative in the middle of the day (I have to pay the utility company to take my electricity) by charging the car at home I save money there. For rural people with roof space for solar EVs should be a no-brainer, but like many rural areas my district is incredibly conservative (do a search for Barnaby Joyce, my local member) and the populace are convinced they don't drive far enough, they'll catch on fire (mine has an LFP battery, so the risk is low) and that I'll need to replace the battery in a year (even though the battery has an 8 year warranty).

That said, it’s been a long time since I was back in Ohio, so maybe I’ve forgotten what it’s like. You guys are smart, head on down to the comments and let me know what I missed!

#4522. U.S. Forest Service releases Bigfoot files

Published Nov 24, 2026 1:28 PM EST

The United States Forest Service has quietly published a handful of documents related to multiple, decades’ old Bigfoot sightings. While the files uploaded to the agency’s Freedom of Information Act online reading room may not offer definitive proof of the cryptid’s existence, they may help redirect unwanted political conversations at the Thanksgiving table this year.

“I don’t know if I believe in the Bigfoot theory, but the tracks were right there,” an 87-year-old resident of Sanders County, Montana, told his local newspaper in 2003 after discovering some suspicious footprints. “What else could it be?”

Another file also focuses on purported cryptid tracks in the summer of 1982. In that case, park rangers were actually dispatched to obtain plaster molds of footprints reported in Oregon’s Umatilla National Forest.Unfortunately, resource staffer Roger Baker didn’t sound impressed by what he found on June 17, 1982.

“It is my opinion that the tracks…were made by something other than a 300-pound-plus, two footed being,” Baker explained, although he did concede that the prints appeared “very natural.”

The final archival document is a local resident’s somewhat rambling personal account of the history of Petty Creek, a forested area located about 30 miles west of Missoula, Montana. Among stories of ill-fated gold prospectors, camel importation, and buried treasure, Leo Kinney tells of his own near-brush with Bigfoot. According to Kinney, he and some fellow hunters didn’t actually see the hairy biped walking around, but they saw evidence of its recent presence.

“Tracks, a strong odor, and grunting were observed,” he wrote in 1980.

The U.S. Forestry Service’s archival uploads are fun reads, but many Sasquatch believers are still reeling from the recent release of Capturing Bigfoot. Released in October, the critically acclaimed documentary delves into the story behind the Patterson–Gimlin tape. The controversial home video recording is widely considered the most famous Bigfoot sighting of all time, although the film essentially confirms once-and-for-all that the grainy footage was a carefully constructed hoax.

#4518. Clam discovered living inside of a sea urchin’s throat

🛍️ Live: The best Black Friday deals on stuff you actually want 🛍️

Published Nov 24, 2026 1:36 PM EST

The fact that a new clam species (Vaticinaria gulicola) was discovered where the sun does not shine may be the least interesting thing about this bivalve. V. gulicola lives inside of a deep-sea urchin. The clam appears to have made a little home for itself inside the urchin’s oesophagus, the tube that runs through the center of the urchin’s body and into the intestine. A study recently published in the journal ZooKeys details this highly unusual partnership.

An international team of scientists conducting a deep-sea survey of the Great Australian Bight discovered the clam. The survey studied the seafloor at depths of 656 to 16,404 feet deep and uncovered 66,721 invertebrates representing 1,267 species. About a third of these species are believed to be new to science—including this quirky clam.

They found V. gulicola along the abyssal seafloor at depths of about 13,000 to 16,400 feet. At this depth, sunlight cannot penetrate the water column. During these deep trawls, the team found clams equipped with threads for attaching to a host, but did not see any hosts. Additional searching revealed more clams lodged inside thin, slippery tubes. They analyzed the DNA of these tubes and discovered that they were the oesophagus of the urchin Carnarechinus clypeatus.

“We were absolutely stunned to find this bivalve living inside the throat of a deepwater sea urchin,” Paul Valentich-Scott, a study co-author and marine malacologist at the Santa Barbara Museum of Natural History, said in a statement.  “A Russian scientist [Alexander Mironov] originally thought these clams were being eaten by the sea urchin, but we later determined that it was actually living inside the oesophagus.”

Mironov had noticed clams inside the urchin’s gut as far back as the 1970s and 1990s. The team also found related clams living inside of a specimen of the same urchin that was collected during the Challenger Expedition (1872 to 1876), where they had gone unnoticed for over a century.

Most clam species that live with other animals cling to the outside of their host. Endocommensalism, or living inside of the host, is more rare. The new clam’s genus Vaticinaria is only the second clam genus of its superfamily known to live this way.

“Endocommensalism is extremely rare in galeommatids and all bivalves,” Valentich-Scott added. “Most commensal bivalves attach to the outside of their host. This new species lives inside its throat.”

This new clam shows no obvious adaptations to life inside a host. It is about 0.74 inches long, which is large for its group, and has a shell that closes fully. The species name gulicola comes from the Latin word for “throat” and “inhabitant.” Much about the clam remains unknown and will require further study.

“We know very little about this new species or its sea urchin host,” said Valentich-Scott. “The host sea urchin has never been collected intact, so we really don’t even know what it looks like. We have no idea how this bivalve can live inside the throat of the urchin, or what it eats.”

The team suspects that the clams can feed off the nutrient-rich sediment that the urchin eats, but this hasn’t been studied. Further deep-sea sampling should reveal more about this clam and other unusual creatures of the deep-sea.

#4517. Rumor: Hyundai is getting ready to roll out an all-new, all-electric work truck

The last time Hyundai announced a new work truck was 22 years ago, and the Hyundai Porter has proven itself as a dependable workhorse throughout Korea and Southeast Asia – but only the pyramids and the Chevy Express can last forever. Hyundai is reportedly getting ready to pull the wraps off an all-new Porter pickup. This time, it’s electric.

Distinct from the Piaggio-branded Porter pickup that’s already sold in Europe, the Hyundai Porter is a conceptually similar, work-focused vehicle with a dropside pickup “bed” trailing a box-like passenger cab and a serious, professional-grade payload capacity.

Carscoops recently published photos of a heavily camouflaged Hyundai Porter prototype last month, along with claims that Hyundai means to follow up the success of sister brand Kia’s multifunctional PV5 electric vans with a globally available electric version of the truck as early as next year. This week, the wraps came off, giving us our best look yet at what the truck might look like when it makes its official debut.

After feeding as many spy shots as I could into some AI models, we ended up with the images you see here. If they’re accurate, they show a commercial-ready EV that’s meant to attract new fleet buyers looking to ditch diesel in Western markets while serving as a direct, 1:1 replacement for domestic fleet operators already putting Porter pickups to work.

Those operators will probably feel a little safer behind the wheel of the new truck, too. Hyundai has worked a short hood and crash structure into the bodywork where a conventional “flat” cabover now sits – a move that seems to point both to a commitment to provide better front-end protection to the truck’s occupants and an intent to at least take an honest run at the Euro NCAP crash standards.

Beyond that, we don’t really know anything about the upcoming Korean pickup – but it’s a safe bet that the next-generation Porter will benefit from some of the technology that’s been baked into the Hyundai Motor Group’s E-GMP.S commercial vehicle platform that underpins the Kia PV vehicles. Those ship with 51.5 and 71.2 kWh battery options sending electrons to 120 kW (~160 hp) electric motors, and while that’s far from a guarantee, it’s not nothing, either.

That’s my take, anyway – what’s yours? Will the Hyundai Porter EV make its way to the West on an AWD version of the E-GMP.S platform, or will it remain a regional model running on one of the company’s hybrid platforms? Let us know in the comments.

This is how EV trucks should look, like this and Telo. Stick storage space under the bed like the T2 Transporter.

SOURCES: SH Proshots, Baldauf, via Carscoops, SEMA News.

#4516. The Porsche 718 Boxster EV Does a Convincing Impression of a Sports Car

An early taste of Porsche’s electric convertible in prototype form excites but raises some tough questions.

The most important detail about the electric Porsche 718 Boxster isn’t that it’s an EV, it’s that it’s a Porsche sports car. The new electric sports car will be officially unveiled next month, but before then, Porsche is offering up a few details on a black-and-red-camoed platter. More important, beyond the limited intel, I got to spin laps in a prototype at the Porsche Experience Center Los Angeles. I also rode shotgun while an engineer hotfooted it through the Angeles National Forest.

I won’t keep you in suspense. As antithetical as an EV might be to the point of a Boxster, this 718 looks, dances, and even sounds (on the inside) like the flat-six-powered machine we’ve known and loved for years. What Porsche put together is an electric car that tries harder than any before at copying the experience of a mid-engine sports car. And there’s a lot more to it than just fake noises.

Where Porsche put the 800-volt battery pack in the Boxster flips the “every EV drives the same” trope on its side. Instead of the industry-standard floor-positioned battery pack, the 718 stuffs it exactly where the internal-combustion engine was traditionally housed in the Boxster: right behind the driver’s head. This changes the weight balance from the EV-typical 50/50 to a much more mid-engine-sports-car-like 40/60. The car’s polar moment of inertia is undeniably behind you, a new sensation in the world of electric cars. Maserati planned something similar for the MC20 Folgore but canceled that project before it made production.

Other big benefits come with this battery arrangement. Engineers have been able to position the seats just as low in the floor as in the gas-powered Boxster, maintaining a proper sports-car driving position. I can promise nobody will be begging for it to be lower. It helps the design too. While this prototype was covered in camouflage, it was evident that there wasn’t a thick battery pack ruining the Boxster’s proportions. Also unaffected by the transition to electric power are the Boxster trunk and frunk. Just by eyeballing them I could tell that they look to be nearly identical to the previous car in terms of capaciousness.

Deciding how large the battery pack should be was one of the biggest problems Porsche had to solve. We’ll need to wait for the reveal to know the car’s range and battery capacity, but everything is a trade-off when it comes to an electric sports car. All we know about its curb weight is that an “intelligent lightweight construction” will yield a vehicle weight “similar to current 911 models.”

For reference, a 911 GTS Cabriolet currently comes in around 3700 pounds. After many, many laps around the Porsche Experience Center, my gut tells me the Boxster weighs somewhere in the 3700–4000-pound range. Or, in other words, exceptional for an EV. And not so great compared with the outgoing 718 GTS 4.0, which managed to weigh in under 3200 pounds.

Without range figures to go by, my only reference point for expectations was that the car flashed a “be mindful of range” warning after about 40 minutes of push laps on Porsche’s track. There are plenty of gas-powered sports cars that would be needing a fresh tank at that point too, although obviously not 911s equipped with the extended-range fuel tank.

Audible entertainment is handled by Porsche’s E-Shift system, which will come standard. This virtual simulation of a PDK transmission and engine noise debuted in the Taycan, and the new Boxster is equipped with its own version of the software. Press the button on the steering wheel, and the naturally aspirated flat-six from the 981-generation Boxster GTS springs to life over speakers both inside and outside the car.

Engineers painstakingly measured, recorded, and reproduced the sound, then emulated a seven-speed PDK for you to shift through. Unlike the Hyundai Ioniq 5 N or the Genesis GV60 Magma, Porsche does not simulate a gas engine’s torque curve in E-Shift, preferring to maximize performance over experience. That said, there are still some theatrics to be found. Downshifting supports “engine” braking via electric-motor regen, and you even hear the “exhaust” popping and crackling on the overrun.

For many Porsche enthusiasts, it won’t be enough, especially when you remove the roof. The speakers are smart in that Porsche is able to simulate the noise as though it’s coming from behind you in traditional mid-engine fashion. But the spell is easily broken when the wind overpowers the speakers, or you gun it past a wall and there’s no delicious mechanical flat-six howl echoing back at you. It’s fake. I could tell straightaway. And everyone else will too.

But alas! I had exponentially more fun driving the Boxster with E-Shift than without, especially on the track. You can choose between manual and automatic gearchanges, and I largely left it in automatic. Hearing and remembering where the “engine” revved as I approached the braking zone helped me learn the track quickly and pick out my braking points by sound alone, very similar to Road & Track’s first experience in the BMW M3 EV prototype running a comparable system.

Then on corner exit, it supplied a faithful throttle reference that helped me trace little slides out of tighter turns in the permissive PSM Sport traction mode. As soon as I turned E-Shift off, I felt lost on the track. And call me old-fashioned, but silently skittering between corners with just the sound of tire squeal is sad. Even more so, because this chassis is a damn good one.

Porsche is being coy with the finer details but let on that numerous chassis components are based on those found in the 911. Boxster owners will be familiar with this hand-me-down strategy, and it continues into the electric era. The steering, braking system, and wheel-and-tire combinations are based on the 911. Pirelli P Zero R summer tires were fitted to staggered wheels (20s in front and 21s in rear) for my time in the car, with a 255-section width in front and a 305-section width in the rear. The new car has PASM damping tech, and engineers note both the damper and spring calibration are softer than those in an equivalent 911. The suspension’s controlled but comfortable composure over rough sections of the road confirmed as much. Thankfully, the brakes just felt like brakes with no weird regen sensation and plenty of feel at the limit.

My test car didn’t have it, but a sport suspension will also be available. And for the first time, the 718 gets optional rear-axle steering, not to help tighten its turning radius but to supply greater stability at high speeds where the rear wheels can turn in coordination with the fronts. There’s even a front-axle lift, picking up where the Spyder RS left off as the first Boxster with said feature.

The powertrain itself is all good news. Porsche wouldn’t supply an output number, but the car I drove employs a single electric motor in the rear. It’s reportedly powerful enough for a 0–60-mph run in under three seconds. Porsche says it will be the most powerful 718 so far, meaning more than the 493-hp output of the GT4 RS, and it will almost certainly be the quickest to 60 too. As with Porsche’s other EVs, there’s a push-to-pass mode you can activate for 10 seconds at a time, and using launch control unleashes maximum output too. But at no point was I wanting for more punch around the relatively tight track. Once the tires warmed, launching was effortless, and I didn’t doubt the sub-three-second claim for a moment. The same goes for the road drive, where the Boxster is powerful enough to need serious restraint to not end up doing jail speeds.

Porsche Torque Vectoring Plus, another feature derived from the 911, helps dole out power between the two rear wheels to maximum effectiveness. Between this power-distribution system and the Boxster’s happy tendency to kindly bend itself into corners under braking, this 718 has the balance and more jovial nature of the previous one. But another trait carries over: The rear shows a tendency to dance further out than you would expect from an EV with a more typical 50/50 weight distribution. And despite that Porsche puts big emphasis on keeping weight down (it even reduced the charge ports from its typical two to only one), there was no denying that this Boxster felt porkier than before. The difference was most obvious in the tighter corners where the mass couldn’t be disguised and the grippy front tires ultimately surrendered to the sheer weight that is being asked to turn.

Porsche says it will be launching the electric Boxster into the world with two versions to start. While it wouldn’t reveal the trims, I do know that the version I drove will be the spicier of the two, therefore corresponding with the previous Boxster S. I can’t be certain whether it’s a hit or a miss until I experience the final production car, but I can say this is much more than simply an electric powertrain transplant.

It challenges the hard-core among us in ways EVs simply haven’t before, and if it’s not your cup of tea, don’t worry. Porsche will keep making gas-powered performance cars. It’s just a shame that they won’t start under $100,000, where this one is projected to begin.

#4515. Bald eagle Kaydee spotted back at Shadow’s nest

🛍️ Live: The best Black Friday deals on stuff you actually want 🛍️

Published Nov 24, 2026 2:58 PM EST

Turkeys may be getting all of the bird hype this week, but plenty is still going on in the reality show that is the bald eagle (Haliaeetus leucocephalus) world.

Just before the sun rose over Big Bear Valley in southern California on Monday morning, Friends of Big Bear Valley’s (FOBBV) cameras picked up the sounds of eagle chortles throughout the area. The sounds continued as the sun came up over the nest that typically belongs to an internet-famous bald eagle dad named Shadow and his late partner, Jackie.

“Eagles vocalize for many different reasons. It could be to communicate territory, a danger warning, mating, food necessity or merely social contact. Their tone is that of a whistling chatter-like chirp, making it easy to differentiate them with their distinctive, high pitched sounds,” FOBBV writes.

The cameras also picked up two unknown soaring eagles, and some ravens scrounging around in the nest. By Monday afternoon, two bald eagles followed each other onto the Lookout Snag, a tree near the nest. While it is not clear which eagles were there, a familiar face was spotted just before sunset. Kaydee, the four-year-old banded female eagle who has been seen near Shadow since August, swooped onto the nest for the first time in several days.

“Kaydee made a welcome visit to the nest. She poked around a bit, before showing us some beautiful closeups, then exiting through the back porch,” FOBBV says. “We can all agree what a welcome sight it was to see Kaydee. It’s a gentle reminder that if we just wait, there are new surprises each and every day.”

We still do not know if Shadow and Kaydee will mate this season. Shadow has recently been spotted with another female eagle nicknamed Big Beautiful Visitor (BBV) by some fans.  Any eggs are generally laid in January. Viewers can follow Shadow, Kaydee, or any other eagle couple that takes over the nest via a 24/7 livestream.

Kaydee, formerly known as KD1, is a banded female bald eagle that has been spotted in Big Bear Valley following the death of Shadow’s former partner, Jackie. She was born in 2022, about 70 miles away from Big Bear Lake in the Prado Basin between Anaheim and Riverside, California. Coincidentally, her parents are also named Lucky and Ricky like Jackie’s parents, but they are a different eagle pair.

Kaydee was banded as part of the Orange County Water District’s work to track the eagles born in the area. These bands help biologists track and monitor the birds over time. Kaydee currently has a black spot on her head, but that may not be permanent. It’s possible that not all of her white feathers have come in or it could be tree sap or dirt. She also has two small bands on her legs. One is a small metal band, while the other is a lavender band with “KD1” on it.

Kaydee is almost five years old, so she is just about ready to mate.

In January, Jackie laid two eggs in the nest, but ravens destroyed them. She later laid two more eggs that hatched in April and named Luna and Sandy. The name Sandy is in honor of FOBBV’s former executive director Sandy Steers, who died from cancer in February.

On July 17, Jackie was found injured on the ground near Dana Point Park, California. Cell phone video from a witness confirmed that she had an altercation with two other subadult eagles. She successfully fended off the other eagles by turning over and using her talons, but could not fly far away.

She was transferred to the Ojai Raptor Center for care, where she was diagnosed with severe anemia. Her anemia worsened during the first week of August, the Ojai Raptor Center said that she was in unstable condition on August 9.

Jackie died early in the morning on August 10. The necropsy did not reveal a single cause of death, and instead pointed to several factors including severe anemia, bird flu, blood clots in her wing and one kidney, and liver and lung abnormalities.

A memorial service was held on September 5 in Fawnskin, California, along with a second celebration of life called Wings Over Big Bear on October 3. The event featured representatives from FOBBV, the Yuhaaviatam of San Manuel Nation, and more.

Earlier this month, the Ojai Raptor Center announced a “room filled with kindness,” that is covered with thousands of letters, drawings, cards, and well-wishes they have received in honor of Jackie.

#4514. E-quipment highlight: Tadano rolls out 35-ton V320RC electric crane

Developed by Japanese material handling giant Tadano, the 35-ton V320RC wheeled electric pick & carry crane has spent the last few months proving itself at NMG Italia’s job sites, where it’s been handling heavy loads in tight industrial spaces and improving efficiency by 50%. And now, you can buy one.

Developed in collaboration with NMG Italia, the V320RC electric crane has already proven its performance in the field with NMG and during precision setup operations at Marmomac, a trade show dedicated to the marble industry held each year in Verona.

“The (Tadano) V320RC marks a real breakthrough in the pick & carry industry,” reads the official Tadano launch copy. “Rather than an evolution of existing solutions, it introduces a new philosophy, with technologies and features capable of setting new benchmarks in the lifting market. Tadano and NMG Italia continue their collaboration in the field, turning real-world experience into new technological solutions to meet the most advanced demands of industrial lifting.”

The crane itself is a compact, battery-electric pick-and-carry machine with a maximum lifting capacity of 35 tonnes. Measuring just 5 m long, 2.15 m wide and 2.400 m tall (a meter is about a yard, guys – you got this), the V320RC is designed to bring heavy lifting capability into tight industrial spaces where larger cranes struggle to operate.

The new Tadano runs on a 120V, 1,120 Ah li-ion battery pack (that works out to ~134 kWh) and packs a gross vehicle weight of more than 31,150 kg (~34.5 short tones). That number includes 9,500 kg (~10 tons) of removable counterweights that make transport and handling easier for a wider range of customers. Under the hood, a new hydraulic system pairs a variable-displacement pump with what the company calls “an electro-hydraulic control valve” to improve precision and responsiveness while reducing energy consumption.

According to NMG Italia, all that baked-in tech V320RC give them 50% better productivity than competing electric cranes working under equivalent workloads, with enough battery capacity to support several days of operation between charges.

On the in-ear side, the 7Hz x Crinacle Zero:2 remain one of the best ways to hear what wired IEMs can do for about $21. Our list of the best mixing headphones can give you more studio insight.

A one-button turntable that plays nice with Bluetooth speakers and real stereos.

Press play, and it lowers the tonearm, finds the groove, and returns the arm when the side ends, so you never have to cue the record by hand. A switchable built-in phono preamp lets it connect to powered speakers or an amp without extra gear, and aptX Adaptive Bluetooth sends your records to wireless headphones or speakers. At $238, it’s well under the cap on our list of the best turntables under $500.

If the PS-LX3BT above leaves you wanting more, the Sony PS-LX5BT is Sony’s step-up model with more premium components but still a nice price at $398 (was $499.99). Pair either turntable with the Klipsch R-41M bookshelf speakers at $134.47 (was $199) and an amp from the section above for a complete starter system (Klipsch is just one solid option for turntable speakers).

Want to go digital? There are a ton of smart, whole-home, streaming-friendly connected speakers on sale below. We love a compact listening station.

The Sonos Arc Ultra drops to $849 (was $1,099) and delivers Dolby Atmos from a single bar that also anchors a whole-home Sonos system. For a smaller TV or a tighter budget, the Bose TV Speaker is $199 (was $279) and is built to make dialogue easier to follow than a TV’s built-in speakers.

#4512. Ineos Announces Plans to Move Production of Grenadier SUV, Quartermaster Pickup Truck to the United States

The move will bring assembly straight to Ineos Automotive’s largest market.

Back in 2016, Land Rover ended production of the old-school Defender. Ineos CEO Jim Ratcliffe then entered the automotive market to fill the niche with the defiantly old-school Grenadier SUV and its pickup truck counterpart, the Quartermaster. Ineos describes the vehicles as offering “rugged British spirit and design with German engineering rigor.” And soon, the brand will add “American-made” to that mix.

On Tuesday, Ineos Automotive announced it is moving Grenadier and Quartermaster production to the United States. The move will happen in 2028, with production moving to an undetermined location in America; an announcement on that should come within a few months. As part of the shuffle, Ineos Automotive says it will sell its current plant in Hambach, France to Chinese automaker BYD, but the brand will still build Grenadier and Quartermaster vehicles in Hambach while it sets up American facilities.

“Americans have already taken the Grenadier to their hearts, and U.S. policies that have created an incredibly attractive, pro-growth business environment. Setting up production there makes so much sense. It will empower us to invest, expand, and reach even more customers around the world,” Ineos Automotive CEO Lynn Calder said in a statement.

This move should make a lot of sense for Ineos. 70 percent of the brand’s global sales are in the U.S. market, so moving production stateside would leave the brand far less exposed to American import tariffs. The Trump administration has imposed a 15 percent tariff on European Union-built vehicles, and the Quartermaster is subject to the 25 percent “chicken tax,” which dates back to the 1960s and protects the U.S. pickup truck market. Alleviating the tariff burden would allow Ineos Automotive to lower prices further, improve profit margins—or, potentially, both.

Ineos Automotive’s announcement made no mention of the purportedly still-upcoming Fusilier, expected to launch as an EV and range-extended EV later this decade. Initial plans called for Austrian manufacturer Magna, maker of the Mercedes G-Class, to engineer and build the Fusilier at its plant in Austria.

#4511. From equipment to ferries to locomotives, Illinois ports are getting a ZEV makeover

The Illinois Clean Ports Program is putting $104 million behind efforts to help clean up its working waterfronts, funds earmarked for heavy-duty electric equipment assets that includes forklifts, giant reach stackers, switcher locomotives, and the charging equipment needed to support them. There’s even a passenger ferry!

Procurement is now underway for zero-emission vehicles, equipment, and supporting infrastructure at four sites across the state. Administered by the Illinois Environmental Protection Agency (Illinois EPA), Illinois’ Clean Ports Program aims to modernize operations at ports and waterfront facilities in Chicago, the Quad Cities, and southern Illinois’ river port districts.

“Illinois’ waterways are a competitive advantage for the state,” said Illinois Governor JB Pritzker, who was elected to a historic third term on 03NOV. “By modernizing port infrastructure, advancing zero-emission technology, and improving air quality, we are strengthening our economy while building a cleaner future for Illinois.”

Illinois’ Clean Ports Program isn’t just replacing diesel-powered equipment with electric alternatives – instead, the plan also includes Level 2 and DC fast charging, shore power and charging for electrified ships, and comprehensive grid upgrades designed to modernize existing port operations and support the deployment of new electric equipment.

The program takes a holistic approach to port electrification at Chicago’s Illinois International Port District (IIPD), treating energy generation, storage, and deployment as parts of a single connected system. On-site solar helps meet the port’s growing electricity needs while excess power is stored for peak hours, when grid electricity is most expensive. This setup reduces strain on the local grid, and acts as a hedge against rising energy costs.

For smaller public port districts, replacing aging equipment and upgrading electrical infrastructure can be an enormous financial undertaking. The Illinois Clean Ports Program helps make those investments possible, bringing cleaner, healthier, zero-emission technology within reach of terminal operators while preparing the state’s ports for a more competitive freight future.

#4510. Mink braves bears to find food, wins award

🛍️ Live: The best Black Friday deals on stuff you actually want 🛍️

Published Nov 24, 2026 5:10 PM EST

In a break from tradition, the park rangers at Tongass National Forest in southeastern Alaska have awarded one of their 2026 Anan Bear Awards to a completely different animal species. For its tenacity in finding food, a small mink (Neogale vison)  walking around Anan Creek wins the On a Mission Award.

“This little mink was a frequent visitor at the trailhead and the beach in Anan,” the rangers write. “It seemed unconcerned by nearby humans, completely focused on the small crabs and other nibbles it could get ahold of. It was on a mission to eat!”

Tongass National Forest’s rangers are awarding the annual Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears (and a lucky mink) spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory in Alaska over the summer.

Tongass is the largest national forest in the United States and covers most of southeastern Alaska, including the state’s capital city of Juneau. The area also includes Mendenhall Glacier (a popular destination for Alaskan cruises), hiking trails, eagles, and plenty of bears. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska. As such, the creek is a very popular dinner spot among black and brown bears.

According to Friends of Anan, 39 bears are known to feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears (Ursus americanus) and eight brown bears (Ursus arctos). Similar to their chunky counterparts farther to the north in Katmai National Park, the bears return each summer to feast on salmon and teach their cubs how to fish and survive the long winter ahead. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear here has their own antics and quirks.

In addition to the bears and mink, numerous other animals call Tongass home. Bald eagles (Haliaeetus leucocephalus), the Alexander Archipelago wolf (Canis lupus ligoni), and the Sitka black-tailed deer (Odocoileus hemionus sitkensis). Importantly, all five of North America’s Pacific salmon species are found within the forest—Chinook salmon (Oncorhynchus tshawytscha), coho (Oncorhynchus kisutch), pink (Oncorhynchus gorbuscha), sockeye  (Oncorhynchus nerka), and chum (Oncorhynchus keta). These five fish species help feed the bears and other mammals and birds who gather here.

The U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear spotted at Anan, while explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of their behavior.

#4508. Briggs & Stratton keeps the lights on longer with bigger 16 kWh LFP battery

For decades, Briggs & Stratton has helped keep the lights on after the storm with its gas-powered generators. Now, the company is bringing that legacy to the electric age with a new 16 kWh backup battery designed to scale with your growing energy needs.

Briggs & Stratton partnered with Texas-based EG4 to offer an all American-branded solution for battery backup power solution last year, and its stackable SimpliPHI batteries helped make it easy to right-size home battery projects – but those batteries were limited in size, and limited in what they could actually offer. With the launch of the brand’s new, 16 kWh SimpliPHI battery, the company is ready to meet your energy needs … even if those needs take you up to 512 kWh. (!)

For context, the average US home uses about 865 kWh of energy per month, so a 512 kWh battery should theoretically keep your lights on for nearly 18 days after a storm – or provide basic power for your whole block for a weekend, at least!

“This launch represents a significant shift in our battery strategy,” explains Sequoya Cross, vice president of energy storage at Briggs & Stratton. “Our combined resources allow us to bring a competitively priced battery of the highest quality to energy storage installers.”

An onboard battery management system (BMS) and built-in Wi-Fi gateway help to streamline the system’s setup for installers, while the Briggs battery’s automatic inverter sensing technology supports closed-loop communication with Sol-Ark, Solis, EG4, Growatt, Megarevo, Victron, and other leading inverters. Other installer-friendly features include an IP65-rated enclosure allows for indoor or outdoor installation in either ground- or wall-mounted setups without requiring an additional cabinet, and an integrated circuit breaker that allows technicians to isolate the battery during servicing.

The battery itself is rated for 8,000 cycles at 90% depth of discharge, with a charge and discharge rate of 0.5C and an end-of-life capacity of 70%. Briggs & Stratton backs its new battery packs with a 12-year parts warranty that includes labor and travel costs, as well as a US-based tech support service.

The SimpliPHI 16 is available for pre-order now, though pricing was not mentioned in the original press release.

#4505. 11-term House rep who mocked a kid’s letter about EVs has lost her seat (Upd.)

An 83 year old Congressional representative who sent an embarrassing letter to a well-meaning 10 year old constituent on the topic of electric cars and climate change, where she seems to brag about saddling his generation with debt through a recent climate rollback she voted for, has lost her seat.

Update: This article was originally posted on May 14, but we wanted to update it with news of the election result. After a recount, Chuck Hubbard has defeated Virginia Foxx by 330 votes, and will go on to represent NC-5 in Congress.

Christian Mango is ten years old, and was encouraged by his elementary school class to write a letter about a topic of his choice, and mail it to a decisionmaker. Christian chose his Congressional representative, 83 year old Virginia Foxx.

Foxx is an 11-term Congresswoman in North Carolina, one of the most gerrymandered states in the nation, and was expected to win a 12th term in the heavily republican district, having previously proudly touted an endorsement from an enemy of the US who tried to overthrow the government. Her opponent is Democrat Chuck Hubbard, a former journalist and native of the district.

For the topic of his letter, Christian chose electric cars – which is what makes this story relevant to us here at Electrek. Christian laid out several points about EVs, stating that “they’re better than normal cars. They’re better for the environment. They pay less. And there’s no gas.” (All true! well done Christian).

Christian suggested that electric cars could be incentivized with a $5,000 tax rebate – lower than the $7.5k EVs used to get, but better than the $0 they get federally today (compare to the ~$20k in ignored costs that gas cars still benefit from).

Christian went on to suggest action on climate change, stating “maybe there is still a chance for 6.5 million people to not die anymore and for the weather to get better just maybe glaciers stop melting.” Christian was probably referring to the number of people who die from air pollution globally each year (though several estimates suggest that number is actually higher, and Christian did conflate climate and weather… but we’ll give him a pass on this one, his heart is in the right place).

Christian was proud of his letter, as was his mother, Emily Mango, who said “he researched, cited facts, and made good arguments in his essay – an essay that had nothing to do with politics. He was proud of his essay.”

But then he got a response, and that’s when things took a turn for the worse. Christian’s mother Emily angrily shared the response on Instagram, where it gained traction.

Emily said Foxx’s screed was “disrespectful, hostile and unkind” and called it “demoralizing and reprehensible.” She said she had to speak to her son and teach him that this response was “not okay,” and that “nobody should talk to a child like that and nobody should talk to a teacher like that.”

I’d also add that it’s full of disinformation, and that it even seems to brag about the massive debt that Foxx has imposed on Christian’s generation.

Foxx includes six links, all from propaganda publications that deny the science of climate change. 3 are from from WSJ (2 of which are opinion pieces) and 1 is from Fox, both of which are owned by the same climate denier, Rupert Murdoch. 1 is from Washington Times, a tabloid founded by a religious cult (yes, really), and 1 is from another right-wing climate denying publication, National Review.

Notably, none of the six links have anything to do with electric cars.

In the text of the response, Foxx touts republicans’ “all of the above” energy policy, which is ironic given that the party whose energy policy she touts has spent most of the last year forcing broken dirty coal plants open (which they are still doing after ruled illegal) and trying to shut down clean cheap ones. Apparently “all of the above” is code for “fossil fuels and nothing else.”

Foxx’s letter does not directly address the strengths of electric cars, despite them being the subject of Christian’s letter. Notably, EVs actually can receive energy from any generation method, whether it be wind, solar, or even coal or gas – whereas gas-powered vehicles can only use one type of energy, oil. Thus, an “all of the above” strategy should probably find EVs the preferable route for transportation.

But in apparent contradiction to Foxx’s surely sincerely held belief that we should pursue an “all of the above” energy policy – which electric cars would help to achieve – she in fact has voted against EVs when given the opportunity.

Foxx claims in her response that she can’t support tax credits on electric cars, because those go to “mostly people with higher incomes who are able to purchase ‘new’ electric cars.”

But she in fact voted against, and later voted to repeal, incentives which were limited to lower-income-earners and were only available on cars up to a certain MSRP cap. Further, they were available on used vehicles, not just new ones – suggesting that Foxx doesn’t know what she voted against.

Foxx was one of 218 republicans to vote in favor of a ~$4 trillion giveaway to wealthy elites. Her vote raised electric bills and threatened US energy security and surrendered US manufacturing jobs to China. Some of the money given away to wealthy elites in the bill was clawed back from energy efficiency programs that had been going to regular Americans.

Those energy efficiency programs had been instituted by the Inflation Reduction Act, the Biden-era law which established tax credits for EVs and other efficiency rebates. The Inflation Reduction Act was actually revenue positive, which is to say it reduced the national debt (by $238B), rather than adding to it, because of provisions to increase enforcement against wealthy tax cheats.

But most of the IRA was repealed by the bill that Foxx voted for, meaning the US lost out on those deficit reductions. All in all, the bill Foxx voted for would add $4 trillion to the national debt – which, incidentally, is another point Foxx touches on in her response.

In one sentence, she seems to directly mock Christian, telling him that “YOU and your classmates will be responsible for that debt” as part of a warning about the dangers of government debt.

But I read this sentence as mockery, rather than as a sincere warning, given that Foxx voted to add $4 trillion to the national debt, which she, at 83 years old, knows she will not have to pay off. Christian, who is 10, will likely spend his whole life saddled with the debt Foxx voted for.

He will also have to pay for her inaction on climate change, which will have increasingly worse effects on the world Christian will grow up into. Foxx’s generation has already felt the heat, with the massive floods that devastated her state in 2024, from a hurricane that was made 200x more likely due to climate change. Now, imagine how much worse it could get if Foxx’s policies remained in place until 72 years from now when Christian will be her age.

Foxx then closes out the letter with disparaging remarks about teachers, claiming that they are “too interested in indoctrinating you,” and warning Christian about “propaganda.” Which I guess shows where Foxx’s attitude comes from – if she has spent her 83 years never trusting anyone who knows more than her about a topic, that would certainly lead to the ignorance reflected in her letter.

Foxx – who somehow has a doctorate in education and currently sits on the Congressional education committee – could have turned this into a nice moment to teach the child who wrote her something about democracy and responsive government, but instead turned it into a moment to teach the world what’s wrong with her.

When we first wrote this article in May, Foxx had a projected 97% chance of winning in a district which voted for her by a 19% margin in 2024.

But that was before America (and its short memory) was reminded of how incapable republicans are of leading anything.

After a pile of economic crises caused by Donald Trump’s incompetent “leadership,” and his continued participation in an 8-month-and-counting war of choice that is spiking energy prices worldwide, bringing oil profits to record highs (and attempting to distract the news from talking about the Epstein files, which he is heavily featured in and has tried to cover up), America was once again fed up. And his incompetence took his entire party down with him.

Safe republican seats were flipped around the country in the biggest “wave” election we’ve seen in recent times, with the Democrats gaining control of both the House and Senate.

And it looks like Democrat Chuck Hubbard, a Wilkes county native and former journalist, who also ran against Foxx in 2024, will now get his chance to represent the people of North Carolina’s 5th district, after winning by 330 votes in a recount.

The situation in North Carolina is particularly interesting, given that republicans had done an emergency redraw of district lines in an attempt to cheat their way to winning more seats.

Generally, district lines get redrawn after each Census, which happens on the decade mark, rather than mid-decade. But republicans saw ahead of time that they were likely to lose the House due to their unpopularity, and wanted to fudge the numbers in several states instead of going for a fair fight.

So they engaged in Gerrymandering, a process wherein district lines are redrawn to favor a particular political party. The idea is to put as many of your opponents’ votes into a few safe seats as possible, while spreading out your own votes to a wider range of seats that you win each by a small margin.

Foxx’s main argument against Christian’s suggested $5,000 EV incentive, is increasing national debt. Yet in just one tax bill, her approval increases the national debt over 10%. This is not Christian’s “responsibility”, this burden is forced on him, along with climate change.

But it turns out that republicans were even more unpopular than they thought, and as a result, their Gerrymandering backfired. Those narrow margins they sought ended up flipping more seats than would have otherwise flipped, turning North Carolina almost completely blue in what analysts have called a “Dummymander“. (NC-5 itself was not one of the redrawn districts, though – it just swung 19 whole points to the Dems)

After a nail-bitingly close election, Foxx requested a recount. The margin is extremely thin, just 0.12% of votes, but today Foxx called to concede, making it the last decided House race of the election, giving Democrats a 258-seat majority.

Foxx previously vowed to run again in 2028, hoping for a less hostile political environment. She will be 85 years old at the time of that election.

#4501. If you can’t beat ’em: VW to export 300,000 Chinese-built cars per year by 2030

With declining sales, annual capacity cuts approaching a million units, and a wave of affordable Chinese competitors entering Western markets, Volkswagen is facing down its own mortality. Rather than fighting it, the company is leaning in and announcing plans to export roughly 300,000 Made-in-China VWs per year by 2030.

American dealers won’t be getting any Made-in-China vehicles (not at first, anyway), but for Mexican, South American, Middle Eastern, African, and Southeast Asian markets, the shift to lower-cost Chinese manufacturing marks a major strategic pivot. In addition to exporting budget-friendly sedans like the Jetta VA3, Volkswagen is also considering a move to adopt Xpeng’s tech stack for up to 75% of its core European lineup.

The move comes as Volkswagen’s Chinese JVs face a sharp sales decline in their home market, selling just 1.2 million new cars in the first nine months of 2026 (down 35% compared to last year). The financial story is even worse, with last year’s roughly $815 million profit falling to a more than $120 million loss.

“The sharp decline in the overall market in China remains an industry-wide challenge,” said Martin Sander, Volkswagen Group’s sales boss, before adding that VW’s “new, locally developed electric models are beginning to make an impact.”

Add in rising energy costs, continuing software issues, and serious labor disputes with the IG Metall union in Europe, and Volkswagen may not have much choice in the matter – which is why it’s not exactly surprising to see VW consider turning China into an export hub. And that 300,000 number? That may be just the start.

On Volkswagen’s third-quarter results call, CFO Arno Antlitz reportedly called that 300,000 annual export target “conservative,” adding that overseas shipments could help offset the carmaker’s weakening prospects in China.

If it's good enough for Apple, then absolutely. Just put "Designed in Germany" instead of "Designed in California" on the back.

Hopefully, though they'll work towards "re-shoring" once they've got through this crisis. Certainly the European governments should support EU based firms importing EU-designed vehicles, so long as there is a plan to supply demand domestically. They should also encourage Chinese firms to build in the EU. Why transport vehicles such a long distance.

Here’s hoping those export plans eventually expand to the US. After years of pushing upmarket, seeing a reborn electric Jetta on US lots would feel like a true return to Volkswagen’s affordable and accessible “people’s car” roots.
